# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
# Review: "Two Years On" (Varden 24-Month Follow-up and Halden Subset)

This is a good follow-up report. It does what the earlier documents called for:
- A registered mediation test, filed before the 24-month outcomes were known.
- A second hours measure from system logs.
- A two-year horizon.
- Plain reporting that the counter arm was stopped.

Its rebuttals of the re-analysis and the meta-analysis are mostly well founded. The point about the meta-analysis's four long-follow-up studies (all uncontrolled, all using scheduled hours) is decisive, and it is what the meta-analysis's own moderator results would lead you to suspect.

The main problems are these:
- The Summary compares figures from two different hours measures.
- Contamination of the control group can explain part of the apparent fading.
- The log-hours measure is not defined clearly enough to support the mediation result.
- The Summary claims more for the mediation analysis than the Limitations section allows.

**Arithmetic.** The per-hour figures check out. 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8%, and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%. Both intervals are essentially the per-FTE interval divided by the hours ratio. The mediation shares sum to 100%. For the Halden subset, 0.968 / 0.866 gives +11.8%, and 34.9 / 40.3 gives −13.4%.

## 1. The Summary compares two different hours measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is based on timesheets and 8.5% on system logs.

| Comparison | Change in gain | Relative decline |
|---|---|---|
| Like-for-like (timesheets): 12.5 → 9.8 | −2.7 points | about 22% |
| Mixed (timesheets → logs): 12.5 → 8.5 | −4.0 points | about 32% |

Section 5 then says the gain "declined by about a quarter," which fits neither figure exactly. The Summary should report 12.5 → 9.8 on timesheets, and give the 8.5% log figure separately as the stricter 24-month estimate.

Also, the intervals at 9 and 24 months overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2. A decline is the most likely reading, but the data don't establish one. The authors' wording, "consistent with some fading," is right. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" should be hedged the same way.

## 2. Control offices that cut meetings bias the 24-month estimate downward

The "unplanned observation" matters for more than its own result. From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings and gained about 4.1% in output per hour. That raises the control-arm average by roughly 1.2 points (2/7 × 4.1). The difference-in-differences estimate falls by about the same amount.

So something like 1.2 of the 2.7-point decline may be the control group improving rather than the treated offices fading. The decay estimate should be reported with and without those two offices, or with an adjustment for them. The authors should also say whether the meeting audit was prompted by what was happening in the treated offices, since that would be a spillover between arms.

## 3. What do system logs measure?

The authors describe log time as "time staff are working on cases" and call it "the stricter measure." Several things need clarifying:

- **Are meetings included?** If log time covers only case-system work, it excludes meetings. Treated offices cut meetings by about 3.5 hours a week more than control offices did. Non-meeting time in treated offices should then have fallen by only about 4% relative to control:
  - Timesheet hours: 37.9 → about 33.4.
  - Meetings: 7.4 → 3.9.
  - Non-meeting time: about 30.5 → 29.5.

  A fall of 11% in log hours is hard to reconcile with that, unless log time is a small or non-proportional share of non-meeting time.
- **Logs and timesheets are not nested.** Logs pick up unclaimed work done on the system. They miss off-system work, such as phone calls, reading, and meetings if those are excluded. So "stricter" is only true in one direction.
- **This affects the mediation result.** Suppose meetings are excluded from the denominator. Then cutting meetings does not directly raise output per log hour. It adds log hours. A 47% share through meetings would then have to work through focus or fewer interruptions, not through freed time. That is an interesting finding, but the paper should say it is the mechanism being claimed.

Please define log time precisely and say whether meeting time is in the denominator.

## 4. The mediation analysis

- **"Confirms" overstates it.** The Summary says the registered test "confirms" that meetings account for 47% of the gain. But the Limitations section says, correctly, that the decomposition assumes no unmeasured confounding between the mediators and the outcome. That assumption cannot be tested. "A registered test supports" would be accurate.
- **The sample is still small.** "A larger sample of office-months" does not mean more independent units. There are still 14 offices. The paper should say how clustering was handled, because intervals of 28–66% seem narrow for 14 clusters. The few-cluster corrections raised for the nine-month report apply here too.
- **The two mediators may not be separable.** Fewer meetings could reduce fatigue. The 47 / 18 / 35 split assumes the two pathways are separable and additive. Say which decomposition method was used and whether the results change with the order of the mediators.
- **Where did baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. The source should be stated, for example calendars retrieved after the fact.
- **Fatigue.** The 0.34 SD improvement is reported without an interval.
- **Timing of registration.** The analysis was registered at month 11, after the nine-month results and the exploratory meetings correlation were known. It was still filed before the 24-month outcomes, so it is properly confirmatory for those outcomes. It would help to say that the model's specification was informed by the earlier exploratory result.

## 5. Problems carried over from the nine-month report

- **Backlog and deadlines.** Output per FTE has stayed about 3% below control for two years. Unless incoming cases fell, the backlog should have grown. Queue size, case age and the rate of statutory-deadline breaches are still not reported. The nine-month report named this as a risk to check at follow-up.
- **Quality, sickness and resignations.** These are still reported as levels in treated and control offices, without intervals or difference-in-differences estimates.
- **The trajectory.** Two time points cannot show whether the gain has levelled off or is still falling. On timesheets, a straight-line continuation would reach zero only around month 75, so stabilisation is plausible. But monthly system data exist and should be plotted.

## 6. Counter arm

Stopping the arm is reported honestly. One figure needs explaining. Twelve percent more staff to restore service would raise staffing cost by about 12%. Total cost per contact would rise 9% only if staff make up about three-quarters of total cost. State the assumption.

## 7. Halden subset

- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations did not respond. Organisations that reverted are plausibly less likely to respond, so 3 of 14 probably understates the reversion rate.
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the Summary's description.** The Summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations." A marketing agency citing client deadlines is discretionary work by the meta-analysis's definition, not coverage-bound. That makes it a more interesting case: a discretionary organisation that found the schedule unworkable. The Summary shouldn't fold it into the coverage story.
- **When did they revert?** The original pilot had five reversions: three retail and hospitality, two healthcare administration. Are the hospitality group and retail chain among those five, or are they later reversions? The marketing agency must be a new one.
- **Which baseline?** The 40.3-hour baseline is the figure from the re-analysis's 27 time-tracking organisations. The 11 continuing organisations should be compared with their own baseline.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** Without a comparison group, economic conditions could push the estimate either way. "Likely optimistic" is accurate. "Upper bound" is not.
- **The attrition misstatement.** The original working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase." The re-analysis showed seven came after the schedule began. With a Halden author on this report, this would be a natural place to acknowledge that and correct it.

## 8. Bearing on earlier claims

Section 5 is fair to both papers:
- The rebuttal of "entirely an artifact" holds. The 8.5% estimate (3.4 to 13.8) meets every standard the re-analysis recommended for case-processing.
- The point about the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies is decisive.

One small point. The re-analysis's month-ten extrapolation was about Halden volunteers, not Varden. "Not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten" is a fair rebuttal of the general claim, but say that the extrapolation came from a different population.

## Suggested revisions

1. Make the Summary compare like with like (12.5 → 9.8 on timesheets), and hedge the decline.
2. Report the 24-month estimates with and without the two control offices that audited their meetings.
3. Define log time and say whether meetings are in the denominator. Reconcile the −11% figure with the meeting cuts.
4. Change "confirms" to "supports." Report how clustering was handled, the decomposition method, and the source of the baseline calendar data.
5. Add backlog and deadline-breach data, a monthly trajectory, and difference-in-differences estimates with intervals for the secondary outcomes.
6. Correct the description of the Halden reverters, use their own baselines, and replace "upper bound."
7. Acknowledge the Halden attrition misstatement.

## Where the evidence now stands

These points update the synthesis I gave after the meta-analysis:

- **Discretionary, backlog-type work.** The gain in output per actual hour is about 8–10% at two years. It is smaller than at nine months, though part of that drop may come from the control group changing. Output per worker is about 3% lower. Whether the backlog is growing has not been reported.
- **Coverage-bound work.** The counter arm was stopped because of waiting times. Restoring service would need about 12% more staff. Evidence for this kind of work is now fairly consistent.
- **Mechanism.** Registered but assumption-dependent evidence favours fewer meetings (about half of the gain) over reduced fatigue (about a fifth). Two control offices that cut meetings without cutting hours gained about 4%. The open policy question is whether reorganising alone captures most of the gain, or whether the cut in hours is what makes reorganisation happen and stick. Only a trial with an arm that reorganises without reducing hours can answer it.
